item.title: Ubuntu shows off an early version of its AI-powered launcher as it plans to integrate LLMs into the OS
item.itunes:title: Ubuntu shows off an early version of its AI-powered launcher as it plans to integrate LLMs into the OS
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Summary

  • Ubuntu previews an optional AI-powered launcher that centralizes AI tools into one hub.
  • LLM features are opt-in, run locally, avoid huge installer downloads, and respect privacy.
  • Security-focused design includes sandboxing; community testing is expected in January.

LLM usage has been one of the biggest sources of discourse in the Linux community in 2026. We've seen some distros open their doors to AI, and others still barring any submissions that contain anything generated by an LLM.

However, from pretty early on, Ubuntu has been clear that it's pro-AI. In fact, it declared its stance back in April, saying that it was more interested in making features that use AI for accessibility than simply 'because it can'. Now, an Ubuntu developer has given us a sneak peek at what we can expect from the distro's future AI plans.

Ubuntu shows off an initial look at its AI-powered launcher

As always, it's totally optional to use

Credit: Ubuntu

Over on Ubuntu Discourse, Didier Roche-Tolomelli of Canonical's Ubuntu Desktop team showed off the first working version of their AI-powered launcher, giving us a little bit of a peek into what the fully-fledged version will look like. It's worth noting that previous footage of this tool was called "warty-prototype" and was an "automated UI simulation" to spark discussion over its implementation. However, what Roche-Tolomelli is showing off right here is an early working version.

It looks like it'll offer a one-stop shop for all your AI features. You can prompt it right there within the launcher, and the post mentions that it's designed to collect all future AI tools into one hub instead of having them scattered all over the place. Roche-Tolomelli hopes to have something ready for the community to test this coming January.

Fortunately, it seems Ubuntu hasn't forgotten what it promised with LLM integrations when it first declared it was experimenting with AI. The LLM-enhanced features are opt-in, and it won't add gigabytes of AI-based data to the installer. It'll run locally, respect your privacy, and come with some nice security features, like a sandboxing architecture.

The Linux community's next big fight isn't about Wayland anymore; it's about whether AI belongs in your distro

Where do you stand?

12
By  Simon Batt

item.title: I compared DLAA, DLSS Quality, and native TAA, and the winner wasn't obvious
item.itunes:title: I compared DLAA, DLSS Quality, and native TAA, and the winner wasn't obvious
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Back when I used to chase 4K gaming, I believed that native rendering was the only way to get the best possible image quality. You can't really blame me for that when early iterations of DLSS made games look like someone smeared Vaseline all over my screen. It wasn't until last year, with DLSS 4, that upscaled footage finally looked comparable to native 4K and convinced me to start using it way more often. In fact, I still remember Nvidia claiming that it could look better than native rendering.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

That claim made me wonder how much of those improvements had to do with the way DLSS handles anti-aliasing rather than upscaling itself. Many games these days force temporal anti-aliasing (TAA), which isn't exactly ideal for image clarity. But when you use DLSS, you're replacing the game's anti-aliasing implementation with Nvidia's. So, you'd think DLAA, which is essentially DLSS without upscaling, would look even better. Spoiler alert: it does, but by how much, and at what cost?

Nvidia says DLSS 4 looks better than native resolution — let's separate fact from fiction

It sounds like nonsense, but Nvidia has a point.

17
By  Jacob Roach

The loser was obvious, though: TAA

It's become a necessary evil in modern gaming

A decade ago, TAA was considered a compelling alternative to MSAA. It was far less taxing on the GPU and did a great job of reducing shimmering. But we've gone from having TAA as one of the options alongside MSAA, SMAA, and FXAA to not even being able to turn it off in many games. That's partly because games these days are developed with the expectation that TAA will help clean up noise from rendering techniques like screen space reflections (SSR), ambient occlusion, and global illumination.

The problem with TAA is that it blends information across multiple frames, so finer details tend to appear less defined than they should, especially in motion. Take a look at the palm trees in my 007 First Light comparison. Notice how the individual leaves appear fuller and more defined with DLSS Quality and DLAA? That's while standing still. With TAA, they start to blur together when I move around. So, even though I'm rendering the game at native resolution, the image ends up looking softer than it does with DLSS Quality.

It's a tough call between DLSS Quality and DLAA

At this point, you're chasing the last few percent of image quality

Now, don't get me wrong. Just like TAA, DLSS and DLAA are both temporal anti-aliasing techniques in the sense that they rely on information from previous frames. But Nvidia uses a trained neural network to reconstruct the image, which does a better job of distinguishing finer details from aliasing artifacts. So, you don't get the same "smoothed-out" effect. If you compare DLSS Quality and DLAA, the difference in detail isn't as pronounced despite the former upscaling from 960p to 1440p.

You may not be able to spot it in the screenshots, but the overall image looks just a tad sharper. I have to look at the thinner branches of the trees to really tell the difference. That's not something I ever do once I actually start playing the game. What I do notice, though, is the FPS hit, which is around 20–40%, depending on the game and how GPU-bound I am. In Cyberpunk 2077, my frame rates dropped from over 80FPS with DLSS Quality to under 50FPS with DLAA. In 007 First Light, I went from 45 to 35FPS with path tracing enabled.

DLAA is still worth it when you have the headroom

But I wouldn't lower other graphics settings just to use it

That FPS tax might be a dealbreaker for many of you, but I do actually use DLAA sometimes. Not because I'm chasing the best image quality at all costs, but because it's perfect when you're CPU-bound. If your GPU usage is low, you won't have to sacrifice as much performance. In Battlefield 6, for instance, my frame rate only dropped by about 12%. Enabling DLSS Quality, on the other hand, barely improved my numbers compared to native TAA at 1440p, so I may as well use DLAA and get that extra detail.

Unfortunately, I don't have that kind of GPU headroom in most of the AAA titles I play these days, even with an RTX 4090 at 1440p. I don't mind using DLAA if I'm able to hit around 100FPS, but I'm not going to dial down graphics settings just to get there. For instance, I'd much rather play Cyberpunk 2077 with DLSS Quality and path tracing than disable the latter and play with DLAA. Any headroom my GPU has is better spent on improving the lighting, shadows, or reflections than making an already sharp image look even sharper.

It all comes down to what you're chasing

For me, the choice is between DLSS and DLAA because at no point during my testing did I feel like native TAA was worth using over DLSS Quality. Even if I'm CPU-bound and get only a 10% FPS boost, I'll still take it because I'm also getting better anti-aliasing. As for DLAA, if you're already exceeding your FPS target at native resolution, I don't see why you wouldn't want to use it and get a sharper image. But considering how hard it is to tell the difference between DLSS Quality and DLAA without actively looking for it, you're probably better off sticking to the former unless you're CPU-bound and you know the FPS hit isn't outrageous.

I stopped using the default DLSS settings, and I don't think I'll go back

But you probably shouldn't unless your GPU has plenty of headroom.

5

item.title: 5 everyday tasks I now do in a browser instead of installing software
item.itunes:title: 5 everyday tasks I now do in a browser instead of installing software
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most of us install software for tasks that come up only once in a while. Over time, those downloads pile up, even when we barely use them. I started looking at browser-based options for some of these everyday needs and found a few that are surprisingly capable. They offer useful features without adding another program to my setup. Here are five online tools that have earned a place in my regular workflow.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

PDF editing

I no longer need a desktop app to handle my PDF tasks

Merging documents, removing unwanted pages, and compressing PDFs are some of the most common document-related tasks I encounter. Yet, handling these simple operations often means installing a dedicated application that takes up space and rarely gets used for anything else.

For most of these tasks, iLovePDF has everything I need in one browser tab. Its collection includes tools for merging and splitting documents, compressing files, rotating pages, adding page numbers, and converting PDFs into other formats. You can also add signatures and password protection when working with documents that need an extra layer of security.

It has become my go-to option for combining documents or removing unnecessary pages. All these operations take just a couple of clicks, without navigating through complicated menus. Unless you regularly work with advanced PDF editing features, iLovePDF covers most of the requirements that come up during everyday work.

iLovePDF

iLovePDF is a popular online platform that provides free and paid tools to merge, split, compress, convert, edit, and sign PDF files.

Check out iLovePDF

File conversion

One website replaced my collection of file converters

With support for hundreds of file formats, CloudConvert covers almost every conversion requirement I encounter. It handles documents, images, audio, videos, spreadsheets, presentations, and even archive files. The process is straightforward: upload a file, select the output format, adjust the available settings, and start the conversion.

CloudConvert also gives you greater control over individual conversions. Depending on the file type, you can adjust parameters such as resolution, quality, and other output settings. Cloud storage integrations are another useful addition, particularly when working with files stored online.

It's useful when I receive an unfamiliar file format or need to prepare documents and media files for different platforms. Instead of searching for another utility, I can handle the conversion from the same interface.

CloudConvert

CloudConvert is an online, browser-based file conversion and utility platform that allows users to convert, merge, or optimize files across over 200 different formats without installing local software.

See at Official Website

Image editing

Photopea handles more than just basic image edits

Working on articles often involves making small changes to screenshots, resizing images, or adjusting thumbnails before publishing them. Not every task calls for Photoshop, but I still want more control than basic image-editing websites offer.

The editing interface in Photopea feels surprisingly familiar, especially if you've previously worked with Photoshop. It includes layers, masks, selection tools, blending options, and filters, along with support for formats such as PSD, PNG, and JPG. You can access these features directly through your browser rather than installing a full-fledged image editor.

Its PSD support is useful when I need to revisit an existing design. You can open an existing project, modify individual layers, adjust selections, and export the finished image without needing Photoshop installed. It also goes well beyond basic cropping and resizing, making it suitable for more involved editing tasks.

I wouldn't replace a professional desktop editor for demanding projects, but that's not where Photopea needs to compete. Whether I'm preparing article thumbnails, adjusting screenshots, or revisiting an existing design, Photopea has most of the editing tools I need.

Photopea

Photopea is a free online photo and graphics editor that's designed to mimic the Photoshop experience for those who want a free alternative.

See at Photopea

I thought cancelling Microsoft 365 would be simple until I had to make everything work for five people.

15
By  Yash Patel

File sharing

File sharing without the cloud

Moving files between my desktop and smartphone shouldn't require cloud storage or email. For occasional transfers, I wanted a simpler option that works directly from a browser. LocalSend Web makes the process straightforward. Open its web interface on the participating devices, select the receiving device, and send your files. You don't need to install its desktop or mobile application to use the browser version.

I find it handy for transferring screenshots, documents, and videos between devices. There's no account registration, subscription, or need to create temporary sharing links. LocalSend Web uses WebRTC for peer-to-peer communication, while a signaling server helps establish the connection. It's a convenient way to move files without relying on cloud-sharing services.

LocalSend

LocalSend is an AirDrop alternative that works across all platforms.

See at LocalSend

Flowcharts and technical diagrams

This browser-based whiteboard makes visualizing ideas effortless

When mapping out a process or planning how different tasks connect, I often find a quick sketch more useful than writing everything down. A visual representation makes it easier to spot connections, rearrange ideas, and explain complicated workflows. Excalidraw gives me a simple space to do exactly that.

The open-source, browser-based whiteboard lets you combine shapes, arrows, connectors, and text to create flowcharts, wireframes, mind maps, and technical diagrams. Its minimal interface makes it easy to start sketching without learning a complicated diagramming application.

Unlike conventional diagramming applications that often produce rigid-looking layouts, Excalidraw makes your drawings resemble something you'd sketch on a physical whiteboard. You can export your creations as images and share them with others, making it useful beyond individual brainstorming sessions.

Excalidraw

Excalidraw is a minimalist, open-source whiteboard for creating hand-drawn style diagrams, sketches, and ideas collaboratively in real time.

See at Excalidraw
I tried replacing Microsoft 365 with a vibe-coded app and a popular FOSS toolkit, and only one stuck

I went looking for something new and ended up sticking with a familiar approach to productivity.

8
By  Yash Patel

It's about finding the right tool, not installing more of them

I've realized that a good workflow isn't about having a separate application for every possible task. It's about knowing which tools are worth keeping around and which ones you can do without. These browser-based tools have proven useful in situations where I once looked for dedicated software. I'll still install desktop programs when a task demands more, but I no longer assume that every job needs one.

item.title: Wii emulation has gotten so good that my original console is now the worst way to play its games
item.itunes:title: Wii emulation has gotten so good that my original console is now the worst way to play its games
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Pulling an original Nintendo Wii out of storage and having to hook it up to a modern 4K OLED TV is frustrating. I feel like the nostalgia of playing goes out the window when you factor in the friction of finding adapters for input and looking at a blurry, washed-out 480p image stretched across a high-DPI panel.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

The Wii itself outputs a maximum resolution of 480p via component cables and only 480i over standard composite. Even with external HDMI adapters or hardware mods, you are still working with a lower-resolution frame buffer and the Wii's notorious hardware deflicker filter.

Of course, I love owning the original Nintendo Wii for historical preservation, but the maturity of the Dolphin emulator (combined with modern upscaling, texture packs, flexible controller mapping, and quality-of-life patches) means that running Wii software on a PC, or even a handheld PC, outperforms the original console in visual clarity, responsiveness, and convenience for me.

The upscaling alone is reason enough to switch

I was fed up with the friction

When using Dolphin it makes use of internal resolution scaling. That means you no longer have to play in native 480p; instead, you can experience your games in 1440p or even 4K, which is four to six times the native resolution. Unlike basic TV upscalers that stretch pixels, Dolphin renders the 3D geometry directly at the target resolution, which can reduce aliasing on character models and environments.

You can even bypass the deflicker filter. The Wii features a hardware-level vertical deflicker filter, originally designed to reduce flicker on interlaced CRT TVs, but it adds noticeable vertical blur on modern progressive-scan displays. If you want to leave it on for nostalgia, you can. However, Dolphin also lets you disable the filter cleanly via the disable copy filter option.

The original Wii achieved 16:9 via anamorphic widescreen, meaning it squeezed a 16:9 image into a 4:3 pixel grid and then relied on the display to stretch it horizontally, which further degrades that horizontal sharpness. With Dolphin, it renders true widescreen without horizontal pixel stretching and also offers community-verified widescreen Gecko/AR codes for games locked to 4:3.

There's also the option of post-processing and custom texture packs. These can fix the muddy ground textures common in the Wii era, and custom HD texture packs, which can be loaded via Dolphin's "Load Custom Textures" feature, can replace low-resolution UI elements and environmental textures while maintaining the original art direction of the titles that you're playing. Dolphin builds often use Uber shaders, specifically hybrid Uber shaders, alongside Vulkan and Direct3D12 backends to eliminate the shader compilation stutter that used to plague so many earlier versions of Wii emulation.

You can use your original Wii remote

Or an alternative works too

Originally, I felt so put off by emulating Wii games because of the controllers and peripherals being such a massive hurdle for me. A big part of the Wii for me was using the Wii controller. It's extremely hard to replicate, but with Dolphin you can use a real Wii remote if you want to. There are two distinct ways that it handles these controllers. The first is standard emulated Bluetooth, which works with pretty much any PC Bluetooth adapter and translates inputs cleanly.

You can also use Bluetooth pass-through, where Dolphin takes direct control of a compatible USB dongle, allowing the Wii remote to communicate directly with the emulated Bluetooth module. This unlocks accurate Wii remote speaker audio, seamless third-party accessory support like your Motion Plus adapters, and the ability to sync controllers using the physical red sync button, just like you would on the original console.

Even if you don't have the proprietary wired Wii sensor bar, it's actually just two clusters of infrared LEDs. With a USB-powered IR bar (such as the Mayflash DolphinBar, which also handles Bluetooth pairing out of the box), you've got yourself a fantastic sensor bar alternative. I actually opted to use two lit candles because flames emit infrared light, which the Wii remote's built-in IR camera tracks to calculate where you're pointing.

If using a Wii remote itself isn't for you, then you can opt for modern controller mapping as well, whether that's with a PlayStation/Xbox controller or a Steam Deck. Dolphin decouples motion controls from physical shaking. Using standard controllers, you can map pointer movements to an analog stick, a mouse, or, most effectively, a controller's built-in gyroscope via SDL input APIs.

There were a range of QoL changes when using Dolphin

Some games have 60 FPS patches

Using the Dolphin emulator has felt like a major quality-of-life change when compared to trying to play games on my original Wii console. 60fps Gecko/AR patches can transform 30fps titles into smoother experiences. This is based on you having a host CPU with strong single-threaded performance. Some games are locked to 30fps due to physics ties, but because my monitor has a variable refresh rate, I get consistent frame pacing without the screen tearing or frame drops I would see on the original hardware during particle-heavy scenes.

Another great feature is instant save states. Some Wii games had pretty restrictive save systems, especially certain online-enabled titles like Super Smash Bros. Brawl or Mario Kart Wii, where save files were locked from being copied to an SD card. But Dolphin has unrestricted NAND/save management and instant save states.

The Wii hardware just doesn't stack up

Unfortunately, the physical reality of my 20-year-old Nintendo Wii is that the hardware is outdated and doesn't provide the nostalgia I was hoping for. Alongside this, there's the chance of failing optical disc drives (specifically dual-layer read issues on games like Super Smash Bros. Brawl), as well as degrading thermal pads and aging capacitors.

If you are looking for the authentic living room party setup, then the original console might still do that for you, particularly if you're relying on peripherals like the Wii Balance Board and you don't want to deal with troubleshooting Bluetooth adapters.

However, for single-player campaigns, high-definition displays, and modern comfort, the original Wii hardware can feel limiting. Dolphin hasn't just replicated the Wii; it stripped away the 2006-era compromises we were making, turning a legacy console into a sharp, responsive, and flexible platform that fits naturally into my PC setup.

Dolphin

Dolphin allows you to emulate Wii games and play with your original Wii remote or alternative controllers depending on what you prefer.

item.itunes:summary:
When I first started self-hosting, most of my Docker containers were dedicated to improving my productivity, managing files, and experimenting with open-source software. However, it didn’t take long for me to realize that my home server could solve some of the everyday problems my family deals with, too.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

After experimenting with several tools, I settled on five that have made managing my household easier.

These 6 self-hosted apps turned my mini PC into a full home lab, and I run them 24/7

I always fall back to this self-hosted stack.

5
By  Rich Edmonds

Paperless-ngx

My filing cabinet went digital

One of the biggest challenges of managing a household is keeping track of all the paperwork that piles up over time. I used to have my important documents scattered across email attachments, cloud storage folders, and physical drawers. Paperless-ngx helped me bring everything under one roof.

Paperless-ngx is more useful than a traditional cloud storage solution due to its OCR. Whenever I upload a scanned document, it extracts the text and makes the contents searchable. Instead of remembering the exact filename of an appliance invoice, I can simply search for the product name, purchase date, or even a serial number mentioned in the document.

I have also created dedicated tags, document types, and correspondents to organize paperwork for different family members, insurance providers, banks, and household expenses. Thanks to its automatic matching rules and workflows, I don’t have to manually categorize every incoming document, either.

Paperless-ngx has become my household’s digital filing cabinet. Whether I need to check an insurance policy before renewing it or retrieve an old purchase invoice for a warranty claim, everything is only a few clicks away.

Paperless-ngx

Paperless-ngx is a document manager tool.

See at Paperless See at Github

Homebox

Nothing I own goes untracked

Keeping track of everything my family owns is another challenge that I never really addressed until I found Homebox. It’s a self-hosted inventory management tool that lets me create a detailed digital catalog of household belongings. Instead of maintaining a boring spreadsheet, I have a dedicated interface where I can organize everything from electronics and kitchen appliances to furniture and accessories.

I can create different locations for my living room, bedroom, kitchen, and storage areas, then assign items accordingly. Homebox lets me record purchase prices, model numbers, serial numbers, warranty expiration dates, and even attach product images, invoices, and user manuals.

It comes in handy when calculating the total value of my household belongings or keeping track of items stored away for months. While creating an initial inventory requires some patience, maintaining it afterward is effortless.

HomeBox

Homebox is a home inventory management tool.

See at HomeBox

Mealie

What’s for dinner? Problem solved

Deciding what to cook every day is one of those small but frustrating household problems. My family often discovers interesting recipes on websites and social media, only to forget about them a few days later. Mealie has helped me create a centralized digital cookbook while making weekly meal planning much more convenient.

One of my favorite Mealie features is its ability to import recipes directly from websites. I simply paste a recipe URL, and Mealie extracts the ingredients, cooking instructions, preparation time, and images into a neatly organized page.

Mealie goes well beyond recipe management. Its built-in meal planner lets me decide what’s on the menu for the upcoming week. Based on the selected recipe, I can add the required ingredients to a shopping list, which makes grocery shopping more organized.

Mealie is a perfect example of how a simple self-hosted app can tackle everyday friction.

Mealie

Mealie is a recipe manager.

See at Github

Actual Budget

Every dollar knows its destination

Managing household finances is one of the most important responsibilities, and Actual Budget has made the entire process easier for me. Instead of relying on complicated spreadsheets or subscription-based budgeting apps, I now have a dedicated self-hosted solution to track my income, expenses, and saving goals.

Actual Budget follows the envelope budgeting methodology, where I can allocate money to different spending categories before spending it. I have created dedicated categories for groceries, electricity bills, insurance premiums, vehicle maintenance, and other household expenses.

This gives me a clear picture of how much money I have available for each category rather than looking at my bank balance. Actual Budget also offers transaction rules, scheduled transactions, and detailed reports. I can analyze my spending habits, track my net worth, and identify categories where my expenses have increased over time.

The biggest advantage is the peace of mind that comes with self-hosting. Financial information is sensitive, and I prefer keeping it on my own server rather than sharing it with another third-party service.

Actual Budget

Actual Budget is a self-hosted finance management tool.

See at Github

These neat services keep my wallet nice and happy

By  Ayush Pande

Home Assistant

My house runs on autopilot

Home Assistant is one of the most ambitious self-hosted apps running on my home server. I like how Home Assistant offers flexibility with automations. Instead of manually controlling individual devices, I can create rules based on specific conditions, schedules, and triggers.

For instance, I can configure my living room lights to turn on automatically after sunset, switch off compatible appliances when everyone leaves the house, and create a bedtime routine that adjusts multiple devices simultaneously.

Home Assistant’s dashboard customization is another highlight. I can create dedicated dashboards for different rooms, glance over temperature readings, check the status of connected appliances, and monitor energy consumption without compatible hardware.

Home Assistant has a steeper learning curve than the other apps on this list. However, once I understood how triggers, conditions, and actions work together, creating automations became much easier.

As you may have already guessed from the name, House Plan lets me create a top-down view of my smart home and arm it with the IoT devices, workstations, microcontroller projects, and other wacky things I’ve added to HASS as entities.

But the real fun began when I started looking into automations involving these entities. A trigger-action pipeline that notifies my phone about the print status was my first automation involving my 3D printing arsenal. However, I recently connected my Spoolman server to Home Assistant using another integration, and after pairing these two packages together via templates and automation rules, I was able to create a workflow that checks the filament consumption metrics for each spool on my 3D printer(s) and uses them to update my Spoolman database.

Pair it with Frigate, and it can summarize entire surveillance streams

With Home Assistant receiving an official llama.cpp integration, I could finally use my locally-hosted AI models as conversation agents on HASS without looking into third-party workarounds. That said, the Gemma 4 E4B (Q4_K_M) model I rely on for productivity tasks also has image analysis capabilities, but I can’t quite use it for my surveillance cameras as is.

That’s where the LLM Vision integration by valentinfrlch comes into the equation. Once I’d connected it to the llama-server instance running Gemma 4, I could have it analyze any frames, screenshots, or even the camera streams from my surveillance setup. I’ve also got a Frigate server running the object detection pipeline on a different PC, which I connected to Home Assistant using its own integration.

Once I’d configured the AI Event Summary blueprint, I was able to put together a pipeline that creates an automated report describing my security camera footage every time Frigate detects an object on the frames.

Proxmox Extended Sensors can pull PVE, PBS, and PDM metrics into Home Assistant

It can pull significantly more entities than the native integration

Technically, Home Assistant currently includes a first-party integration capable of tracking resource consumption stats for my Proxmox nodes and their virtual guests, and I can even use the entities pulled by it in my trigger-action pipelines. I also couldn’t find the S.M.A.R.T. stats for my drives on this integration the last time I tried using it, and its entity list is also somewhat lacking compared to certain third-party integrations.

Meanwhile, the Proxmox Extended Sensors package by Javisen can pull all sorts of entities from my PVE workstations into Home Assistant, including metrics that are simply unavailable on the official integration. Better yet, it can even pair with Proxmox Backup Server and Proxmox Datacenter Manager, on top of supporting multiple cluster nodes.

The Home Assistant Marketplace is laden with cool integrations

So far, I’ve only covered four of my favorite offerings on the Marketplace, but you’ll find dozens of other useful tools hidden in there. The Bubble Card Tools package, for example, includes nested menus to make devices with too many entities less of an eyesore on dashboards, while the Compact Power Card makes it easy to visualize the energy consumption stats of my smart gizmos. There’s also the community-created Amazon integration, which can import shipment details as metrics you can use to automate your smart home.

item.title: I gave my old DirectX 9 games HDR with RTX HDR, and my HDR monitor finally earned its keep
item.itunes:title: I gave my old DirectX 9 games HDR with RTX HDR, and my HDR monitor finally earned its keep
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've spent the last few months staring at my Alienware OLED and wondering whether I was actually getting my money's worth out of it. Sure, modern games can look spectacular on an HDR display, but a surprisingly large chunk of my library predates HDR altogether.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

I'll admit my single-player game library mostly consists of the titles I grew up playing instead of the latest AAA releases, and most of them were built around an era when SDR was the standard. That's what got me wondering what would happen if I dragged them, kicking and screaming, into the modern display era.

So I dug through my backlog for games that were never designed with today's HDR monitors in mind and found five particularly interesting candidates. They're old, they're ridiculously easy for my RTX 4070 Ti to run, and they have absolutely no business looking the way they do on an OLED. That's where NVIDIA's RTX HDR comes in.

I've stopped waiting for native 4K gaming — DLSS upscaling is better

I'd rather play my game than count every pixel.

11
By  Samarveer Singh

DirectX 9 games weren't built for HDR displays

HDR back then didn't mean what it does now

DirectX 9 arrived when SDR displays were the rule, not the exception, so games built around it were never designed to send a modern HDR signal to your monitor. Their color pipelines, tone mapping, and output were fundamentally designed for SDR.

So, if I wanted to play my all-time favorites like Burnout Paradise or Batman: Arkham Asylum in HDR, I'd effectively be asking for a DVD player to understand Dolby Vision.

There are exceptions, of course. Some Source-engine games advertised HDR rendering, but that wasn't HDR output. The engine could calculate lighting with a much wider range of luminance values, then tone-map that information back into an SDR image. The lighting was HDR, sure, but the signal that left the PC never was.

Now, modern monitors support HDR much more easily, but they need actual HDR output to properly use their capabilities. Internal HDR lighting alone can't suddenly make your OLED's highlights brighter or its blacks deeper. That's why these old games are so much more interesting to me than they've ever been. My GPU has so many tricks up its sleeve for my old games that there's always something new to try, be it DLSS 5, RTX Remix, or RTX HDR.

GTA 6 is already running at 60fps with DLSS 5 with the help of a PC, thanks to a clever PS5 Remote Play workaround

This one is for all the PC gamers out there raging over the console-exclusive's 30fps

By  Patrick O'Rourke

RTX HDR makes these old games feel strangely new

My OLED finally had something worthwhile to show me

I bought my Alienware AW2726DM a few months ago, and while the 1440p 240Hz OLED panel has been fantastic, I couldn't shake the feeling that I wasn't using all of it. OLED monitors are getting cheaper, thankfully, but HDR is still one of those features that's easy to forget until something actually uses it properly.

That changed when I fired up NVIDIA App's overlay and enabled the RTX HDR filter. I deliberately started with Burnout Paradise, a game that has no concept of modern HDR, and the difference was immediately ridiculous. Sunlight had actual intensity, bright skies stopped looking like flat white paint, and explosions had a punch that simply wasn't present in the original SDR image.

Batman: Arkham Asylum was even more convincing. Its perpetually gloomy environments gave RTX HDR plenty to work with, and the OLED's ability to make individual highlights explode against genuinely dark surroundings made Gotham feel considerably more atmospheric.

To enable RTX HDR, make sure you have the Nvidia Overlay enabled in the Nvidia App. You'll also need Windows' HDR enabled, and Auto HDR disabled.

Assassin's Creed Brotherhood went in the opposite direction. Its bright Italian streets and sunlit architecture took on considerably more depth, and the highlights looked like they were actually coming from somewhere rather than being painted onto the screen.

Despite these aforementioned games being some of my favorites, I saw the most significant difference when I played a title I never cared too much for — F.E.A.R. 2. Its combination of pitch-black corridors and violent flashes made the HDR effect ridiculously effective. It was the kind of transformation that made me wonder why I had been playing these games in SDR for even a single day after buying my new monitor.

When it came to Black Mesa, the difference was perhaps the most interesting of all. Its Source-engine heritage made it a perfect reminder that internal HDR lighting and actual HDR output are two very different things.

I gave my old PC games path tracing with RTX Remix, and they look better than DLSS 5

There's literally nothing like a lighting overhaul.

1
By  Samarveer Singh

RTX HDR isn't free, but that's hardly a problem here

My RTX 4070 Ti has plenty of frames to spare

RTX HDR does have a performance cost, and pretending otherwise would undermine the whole experiment. The filter needs GPU resources to process the game's output, so you will lose some frames compared with running the same title in plain SDR.

The good news, however, is that these are DirectX 9 games, after all. My RTX 4070 Ti is not exactly fighting for its life trying to render these decade-old games.

Most of these games already run at hundreds of frames per second at 1440p, leaving an enormous amount of headroom for RTX HDR. Losing a small percentage of that performance is practically meaningless when my AW2726DM tops out at 240Hz anyway.

That makes RTX HDR particularly compelling for older games. The performance trade-off that might be difficult to justify in a demanding modern title becomes almost laughable when you're dealing with hardware that far exceeds these games' requirements.

For me, that's ultimately what makes RTX HDR so compelling here. These games don't need more performance, but they sure look better when you give them a modern visual treatment using newer hardware and software tricks.

I used a VR trick to increase my DLSS 5 frame rate, and it's what everyone should be using

DLSS 5 finally learned to cut corners

By  Samarveer Singh

My old games still have plenty left to give

I bought an OLED because I wanted better-looking games, but I hadn't considered that some of the biggest gains would come from games I already owned. Even without tricks like adding RTX Remix, these games, when given deeper colors, can shine brighter than ever, and even take on a new life, years after you played them for the last time.

PC gaming has always been unusually good at refusing to leave old software behind, and RTX HDR gives that philosophy another neat little trick. My OLED isn't just something I bought for the games coming next. It's making the games I already loved feel worth revisiting, and that might be the best use for it yet.

At $125.99, this is the lowest price this lock has ever hit on Amazon, and it is $84 off the regular $209.99 list price. If you have been waiting for a smart lock that handles fingerprint, keypad, and app access without a hub, this is the deal.

item.title: I vibe-coded my own productivity tools to replace the software I used every day
item.itunes:title: I vibe-coded my own productivity tools to replace the software I used every day
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've always found it frustrating when a software tool almost fits my needs but misses a few things that matter to my workflow. Adding another subscription or switching between multiple apps isn't always the answer. With AI coding assistants, there's now another option: building the tools myself. I experimented with this approach and created a handful of small applications and browser extensions to handle everyday tasks using Claude Code (Opus 5.5). Some turned out more useful than I expected.

Add XDA on Google Add as Preferred Source Follow on Google Discover

Budget and expense tracker app

A simpler way to keep my spending in check

Managing everyday expenses shouldn't require navigating a complicated financial dashboard. That's the idea behind Spendwise, a personal budget and expense tracker I created to keep tabs on my spending. Most expense-tracking apps offer more features than I need, and some put basic functionality behind paid plans. This one focuses on the essentials.

Adding a transaction takes just a few moments. I can categorize purchases, set monthly budgets, and see how much I've spent without manually sorting through individual entries. Visual summaries offer a useful breakdown of spending habits, making it easier to identify categories where my money goes. The uncluttered dashboard also keeps important information within easy reach.

I also hosted Spendwise on Vercel, so I can access it from my desktop or phone. This makes it convenient to record purchases on the go instead of waiting until I'm back at my computer. AI handled the development process, including the interface and underlying functionality, turning a simple idea into a working expense tracker.

Personal task management dashboard

A dashboard built around the way I plan my day

My daily workload involves more than keeping a list of unfinished tasks. Projects have deadlines, priorities change, and some responsibilities repeat every week. Cadence addresses these different requirements by combining task management, projects, calendar planning, habits, and notes in one dashboard.

The homepage acts as a snapshot of my workday. It displays active and overdue tasks, upcoming deadlines, completed items, and weekly completion statistics. There's also a Today's Focus area where I can rearrange tasks using drag-and-drop. I can also switch between three views depending on how I want to manage my workload: a sortable task list, a Kanban board, or a calendar with month, week, and day layouts.

Individual tasks come with plenty of room for detail, including priorities, subtasks, descriptions, tags, reminders, and recurring schedules. Projects have their own progress indicators and deadline tracking.

I deliberately kept Cadence local-first. It doesn't require an account, server, or external database. Everything is stored in the browser's IndexedDB, while JSON import and export provide a straightforward way to manage backups. It's a complete personal workspace without the overhead of maintaining a cloud service.

I tried replacing Microsoft 365 with a vibe-coded app and a popular FOSS toolkit, and only one stuck

I went looking for something new and ended up sticking with a familiar approach to productivity.

8
By  Yash Patel

Useful Chrome extensions

Browser utilities for my everyday tasks

Chrome extensions are an important part of my productivity workflow. Whether it's finding information while browsing or capturing screenshots for my articles, I rely on several small utilities throughout the day. However, after running into privacy issues with extensions changing ownership, I decided to take a different route and vibe-code my own alternatives. LensSnap and SnapNest are two such creations.

LensSnap focuses on visual search. It lets me select any part of a webpage, image, or video frame and search for it using Google Lens. There are additional options for shopping searches, copying captures, and saving them as PNG files. A small history panel also keeps recent captures within reach.

When visual search isn't the goal, SnapNest takes care of capturing what's on the screen. It supports region selection, full-page captures, and individual webpage elements. Its built-in editor goes beyond basic cropping, offering gradients, custom backgrounds, annotations, and blur tools. This is particularly handy when preparing images for articles without opening a separate editing application.

Note-taking tool

A better home for connected notes and ideas

Over time, my notes became more than just a place to store random thoughts. I wanted a way to connect ideas, organize research, and quickly revisit information I'd saved earlier. That led me to build Verso, a personal knowledge management app inspired by Obsidian, Notion, Apple Notes, and Craft.

Its rich-text editor supports headings, checklists, tables, code blocks, images, and file attachments. Markdown storage and Obsidian-style wiki links make it easy to connect related notes, while the graph view visualizes those connections. Backlinks, daily notes, reusable templates, nested folders, and tags offer plenty of flexibility for organizing research and personal notes.

Full-text search makes finding older information quick, and the command palette provides shortcuts for creating notes, navigating folders, and managing the workspace. It also supports importing existing Obsidian vaults, making it easier to bring an existing collection of notes into Verso.

4 vibe-coded alternatives of paid apps that can make you re-think your productivity workflow

These underrated vibe-coded projects might change how you work every day.

By  Yash Patel

What started as experiments became part of my routine

Not every feature I build needs to be perfect, and not every experiment needs to replace an established application. What matters is that these projects have given me a better understanding of the software I use every day. I've also discovered how much can be achieved with a clear idea and the right AI coding assistant. It's made experimenting with software far more approachable, even for projects that once seemed too ambitious to attempt.

Browser utilities for my everyday tasks

Chrome extensions are an important part of my productivity workflow. Whether it's finding information while browsing or capturing screenshots for my articles, I rely on several small utilities throughout the day. However, after running into privacy issues with extensions changing ownership, I decided to take a different route and vibe-code my own alternatives. LensSnap and SnapNest are two such creations.

LensSnap focuses on visual search. It lets me select any part of a webpage, image, or video frame and search for it using Google Lens. There are additional options for shopping searches, copying captures, and saving them as PNG files. A small history panel also keeps recent captures within reach.

When visual search isn't the goal, SnapNest takes care of capturing what's on the screen. It supports region selection, full-page captures, and individual webpage elements. Its built-in editor goes beyond basic cropping, offering gradients, custom backgrounds, annotations, and blur tools. This is particularly handy when preparing images for articles without opening a separate editing application.

Note-taking tool

A better home for connected notes and ideas

Over time, my notes became more than just a place to store random thoughts. I wanted a way to connect ideas, organize research, and quickly revisit information I'd saved earlier. That led me to build Verso, a personal knowledge management app inspired by Obsidian, Notion, Apple Notes, and Craft.

Its rich-text editor supports headings, checklists, tables, code blocks, images, and file attachments. Markdown storage and Obsidian-style wiki links make it easy to connect related notes, while the graph view visualizes those connections. Backlinks, daily notes, reusable templates, nested folders, and tags offer plenty of flexibility for organizing research and personal notes.

Full-text search makes finding older information quick, and the command palette provides shortcuts for creating notes, navigating folders, and managing the workspace. It also supports importing existing Obsidian vaults, making it easier to bring an existing collection of notes into Verso.
